title: Chapter 30. Of the Office of the Sovereign Representative
paragraphs: The OFFICE of the sovereign (whether monarch or assembly) consists in the end for which he was entrusted with the sovereign power — namely, the procuring of the safety of the people, to which he is obliged by the law of nature, and is to render account of it to God, the author of that law, and to no one else. By 'safety' here is meant not a bare preservation, but also all the other contentments of life which every man, by lawful industry, without danger or hurt to the commonwealth, shall acquire for himself.

This is intended to be done not by care applied to individuals (beyond their protection from injuries when they shall complain), but by a general providence contained in public instruction, both of doctrine and example, and in the making and executing of good laws, to which individual persons may apply their own cases.
It is against the duty of a sovereign to relinquish any essential right of sovereignty, or to fail to see the people taught the grounds of them.

Because, if the essential rights of sovereignty (specified before in the eighteenth chapter) are taken away, the commonwealth is thereby dissolved, and every man returns into the condition and calamity of a war with every other man (which is the greatest evil that can happen in this life), it is the office of the sovereign to maintain those rights entire; and consequently it is against his duty, first, to transfer to another, or to lay aside, any of them. For he who deserts the means deserts the end; and he deserts the means who, being the sovereign, acknowledges himself subject to the civil laws, and renounces the power of supreme judicature, or of making war or peace by his own authority, or of judging of the necessities of the commonwealth, or of levying money and soldiers when and as much as in his own conscience he shall judge necessary, or of making officers and ministers both of war and peace, or of appointing teachers and examining what doctrines are conformable, or contrary, to the defence, peace, and good of the people. Second, it is against his duty to let the people be ignorant, or misinformed, of the grounds and reasons of those essential rights of his; because thereby men are easily seduced and drawn to resist him when the commonwealth shall require the use and exercise of those rights.

And the grounds of these rights have all the more need to be diligently and truly taught because they cannot be maintained by any civil law, or by the terror of legal punishment. For a civil law that forbids rebellion (and such is all resistance to the essential rights of sovereignty) is, as civil law, no obligation, but only by virtue of the law of nature, which forbids the violation of faith; and if men do not know this natural obligation, they cannot know the right of any law the sovereign makes. As for the punishment, they take it only for an act of hostility, which, when they think they have strength enough, they will try by acts of hostility to avoid.
An objection from those who say there are no principles of reason for absolute sovereignty.

As I have heard some say that justice is but a word without substance, and that whatever a man can by force or by craft acquire to himself (not only in the condition of war, but also in a commonwealth) is his own — which I have already shown to be false — so there are also those who maintain that there are no grounds or principles of reason to support those essential rights which make sovereignty absolute. For if there were, they would (these men say) have been found out in some place or other; whereas we see that until now there has been no commonwealth in which those rights have been acknowledged or claimed. In this they argue as badly as if the savage people of America were to deny that there were any grounds, or principles, of reason for building a house so as to last as long as the materials, because they have never yet seen any so well built. Time and industry produce every day new knowledge. And as the art of building well is derived from principles of reason discovered by industrious men who had long studied the nature of materials and the various effects of figure and proportion — long after mankind first began (though poorly) to build — so, long after men have begun to constitute commonwealths (imperfect, and apt to relapse into disorder), principles of reason may be found by industrious meditation. Whether men make use of them, or neglect them, concerns my own particular interest, at this day, very little. But supposing my principles are not such principles of reason, I am at least sure that they are principles from the authority of Scripture, as I shall make appear when I come to speak of the Kingdom of God (administered by Moses) over the Jews, his peculiar people by covenant.

But they say again that, though the principles are right, common people are not capable enough to be made to understand them. I should be glad if the rich and powerful subjects of a kingdom, or those reckoned the most learned, were no less incapable than the common people. But all men know that the obstacles to this kind of doctrine proceed not so much from the difficulty of the matter as from the interest of those who are to learn. Powerful men hardly digest anything that sets up a power to bridle their affections; and learned men, anything that exposes their errors, and thereby lessens their authority. Whereas the minds of common people, unless they are tainted by dependence on the powerful, or scribbled over with the opinions of their doctors, are like clean paper, fit to receive whatever is imprinted on them by public authority. Shall whole nations be brought to acquiesce in the great mysteries of the Christian religion, which are above reason, and millions of men be made to believe that the same body may be in innumerable places at one and the same time (which is against reason); and shall men not be able, by their teaching and preaching, protected by the law, to make accepted what is so consonant to reason that any unprejudiced man needs no more to learn it than to hear it? I conclude therefore that in the instruction of the people in the essential rights (which are the natural and fundamental laws) of sovereignty, there is no difficulty (so long as a sovereign has his power entire) except what proceeds from his own fault, or the fault of those he trusts in the administration of the commonwealth; and consequently it is his duty to cause them to be so instructed; and not only his duty, but also his benefit and security, against the danger that may arise to himself in his natural person from rebellion.

And (to descend to particulars) the people are to be taught: first, that they ought not to be in love with any form of government they see in their neighbour nations more than with their own; nor (whatever present prosperity they behold in nations governed otherwise than they) to desire change. For the prosperity of a people ruled by an aristocratic or democratic assembly comes not from aristocracy nor from democracy, but from the obedience and concord of the subjects; nor does a people flourish in a monarchy because one man has the right to rule them, but because they obey him. Take away in any kind of state obedience (and consequently the concord of the people), and they shall not only not flourish, but in a short time will be dissolved. And those who, by disobedience, set out to do no more than reform the commonwealth shall find that they thereby destroy it — like the foolish daughters of Pelias in the fable, who, desiring to renew the youth of their decrepit father, did, on the counsel of Medea, cut him in pieces and boil him with strange herbs, but made no new man of him. This desire of change is like the breach of the first of God's commandments: for there God says, Non Habebis Deos Alienos — 'Thou shalt not have the gods of other nations'; and in another place, concerning kings, that they are gods.

Second, they are to be taught that they ought not to be carried away by admiration for the virtue of any of their fellow subjects, however high he stands or however conspicuously he shines in the commonwealth, nor of any assembly (except the sovereign assembly), so as to defer to them any obedience or honour that belongs only to the sovereign (whom in their particular stations they represent); nor to receive any influence from them but such as is conveyed by them from the sovereign authority. For a sovereign cannot be imagined to love his people as he ought who is not jealous of them, but suffers them, by the flattery of popular men, to be seduced from their loyalty — as they have often been, not only secretly but openly, so as to have marriage with them proclaimed In Facie Ecclesiae by preachers, and the same published in the open streets — which may fitly be compared to the violation of the second of the Ten Commandments.

Third, in consequence of this, they ought to be informed how great a fault it is to speak evil of the sovereign representative (whether one man or an assembly of men), or to argue and dispute his power, or in any way to use his name irreverently, by which he may be brought into contempt with his people, and their obedience (in which the safety of the commonwealth consists) slackened. This doctrine the third commandment, by resemblance, points to.

Fourth, since the people cannot be taught this — nor, when it is taught, remember it; nor, after one generation has passed, so much as know in whom the sovereign power is placed — without setting apart from their ordinary labour certain times in which they may attend those appointed to instruct them, it is necessary that some such times be appointed, in which they may assemble together and (after prayers and praises given to God, the sovereign of sovereigns) hear those duties told to them, and the positive laws (such as generally concern them all) read and expounded, and be reminded of the authority that makes them laws. To this end the Jews had, every seventh day, a Sabbath, on which the law was read and expounded; and in the solemnity of which they were reminded that their king was God; that having created the world in six days, he rested the seventh day; and by their resting on it from their labour, that the God who had redeemed them from their servile and painful labour in Egypt was their king, and gave them a time, after they had rejoiced in God, to take joy also in themselves, by lawful recreation. So the first table of the commandments is all spent in setting down the sum of God's absolute power, not only as God but as king (by particular pact) of the Jews; and it may therefore shed light, for those to whom the sovereign power has been conferred by the consent of men, on what doctrine they ought to teach their subjects.

And because the first instruction of children depends on the care of their parents, it is necessary that children should be obedient to them while they are under their tutelage — and not only so, but also that afterwards (as gratitude requires) they acknowledge the benefit of their education by external signs of honour. To this end they are to be taught that originally the father of every man was also his sovereign lord, with power over him of life and death; and that the fathers of families, when by instituting a commonwealth they resigned that absolute power, never intended to lose the honour due to them for their education. For to relinquish such a right was not necessary for the institution of sovereign power; nor would there be any reason why a man should want to have children, or take the care to nourish and instruct them, if afterwards he were to have no other benefit from them than from other men. And this accords with the fifth commandment.

Again, every sovereign ought to cause justice to be taught — which (consisting in taking from no man what is his) is as much as to say, to cause men to be taught not to deprive their neighbour, by violence or fraud, of any thing which by the sovereign authority is theirs. Of things held in property, those dearest to a man are his own life and limbs; and in the next degree (in most men), those that concern conjugal affection; and after them, riches and means of living. Therefore the people are to be taught to abstain from violence to one another's person by private revenges; from violation of conjugal honour; and from forcible rapine and fraudulent surreption of one another's goods. For which purpose, also, it is necessary they be shown the evil consequences of false judgement, through corruption of either judges or witnesses — whereby the distinction of property is taken away, and justice becomes of no effect. All of which things are intimated in the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth commandments.

Lastly, they are to be taught that not only the unjust acts, but also the designs and intentions to do them (even when by accident hindered), are injustice; for injustice consists in the depravity of the will as well as in the irregularity of the act. And this is the intent of the tenth commandment, and the sum of the second table; which is reduced all to this one commandment of mutual charity, 'Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself' — as the sum of the first table is reduced to 'the love of God,' whom they had then newly received as their king.

As for the means and conduits by which the people may receive this instruction, we should ask by what means so many opinions, contrary to the peace of mankind, founded on weak and false principles, have nevertheless been so deeply rooted in them. I mean those opinions which I specified in the previous chapter: that men shall judge what is lawful and unlawful, not by the law itself, but by their own private judgements; that subjects sin in obeying the commands of the commonwealth, unless they themselves have first judged them to be lawful; that their property in their riches is such as to exclude the dominion which the commonwealth has over the same; that it is lawful for subjects to kill those they call tyrants; that the sovereign power may be divided; and the like. These come to be instilled into the people by this means. Those whom necessity or covetousness keeps intent on their trades and labour, and those, on the other hand, whom superfluity or sloth carries after their sensual pleasures (the two sorts who make up the greatest part of mankind), being diverted from the deep meditation which the learning of truth — not only in the matter of natural justice, but also of all other sciences — necessarily requires, receive the notions of their duty chiefly from divines in the pulpit, and partly from such of their neighbours, or familiar acquaintances, as, having the faculty of discoursing readily and plausibly, seem wiser and better learned in cases of law and conscience than themselves. And the divines, and others who make a show of learning, derive their knowledge from the universities, and from the schools of law, or from the books which by men eminent in those schools and universities have been published. It is therefore plain that the instruction of the people depends wholly on the right teaching of youth in the universities. But (some may say) are not the universities of England learned enough already to do that? Or is it you who will undertake to teach the universities? Hard questions. Yet to the first, I do not doubt to answer that until towards the latter end of Henry the Eighth, the power of the pope was always upheld against the power of the commonwealth, principally by the universities; and that the doctrines maintained by so many preachers against the sovereign power of the king, and by so many lawyers and others who had their education there, is sufficient argument that, though the universities were not the authors of those false doctrines, they did not know how to plant the true. For in such a contradiction of opinions, it is most certain that they were not sufficiently instructed; and it is no wonder if they still retain a relish of that subtle liquor with which they were first seasoned, against the civil authority. But to the latter question, it is neither fitting nor needful for me to say either yes or no: for any man who sees what I am doing may easily perceive what I think.

The safety of the people further requires of him, or them, who have the sovereign power, that justice be equally administered to all classes of people; that is, that as well the rich and mighty as the poor and obscure may be righted of the injuries done them — so that the great may have no greater hope of impunity, when they do violence, dishonour, or any injury to the meaner sort, than the meaner have when one of them does the like to one of the great. For in this consists equity, to which, being a precept of the law of nature, a sovereign is as much subject as any of the lowest of his people. All breaches of the law are offences against the commonwealth, but some are also against private persons. Those that concern the commonwealth only may, without breach of equity, be pardoned; for every man may pardon what is done against himself, according to his own discretion. But an offence against a private man cannot in equity be pardoned without the consent of the man who is injured, or reasonable satisfaction.

The inequality of subjects proceeds from the acts of sovereign power, and so has no more place in the presence of the sovereign (that is, in a court of justice) than the inequality between kings and their subjects in the presence of the King of Kings. The honour of great persons is to be valued for their beneficence, and for the aids they give to men of inferior rank, or not at all. And the violences, oppressions, and injuries they do are not extenuated, but aggravated, by the greatness of their persons, because they have least need to commit them. The consequences of this partiality toward the great proceed in this way: impunity makes insolence; insolence, hatred; and hatred, an endeavour to pull down all oppressing and contumelious greatness, even at the cost of the ruin of the commonwealth.

To equal justice also belongs the equal imposition of taxes, the equality of which depends not on the equality of riches but on the equality of the debt that every man owes to the commonwealth for his defence. It is not enough for a man to labour for the maintenance of his life; he must also fight (if need be) for the securing of his labour. Men must either do as the Jews did after their return from captivity, in rebuilding the temple — build with one hand and hold the sword in the other — or else they must hire others to fight for them. For the impositions laid on the people by the sovereign power are nothing but the wages due to those who hold the public sword, to defend private men in the exercise of their several trades and callings. Since then the benefit that every man receives from this is the enjoyment of life, which is equally dear to poor and rich, the debt which a poor man owes those who defend his life is the same as the debt a rich man owes for the defence of his — except that the rich, who have the service of the poor, may be debtors not only for their own persons but for many more. From which it follows that the equality of imposition consists rather in the equality of what is consumed than in the equality of the riches of the persons consuming it. For what reason is there that he who labours much, and sparing the fruits of his labour consumes little, should be more charged than he who, living idly, gets little and spends all he gets — since the one has no more protection from the commonwealth than the other? But when the impositions are laid on the things men consume, every man pays equally for what he uses; nor is the commonwealth defrauded by the luxurious waste of private men.

And whereas many men, by unavoidable accident, become unable to maintain themselves by their labour, they ought not to be left to the charity of private persons but to be provided for (so far as the necessities of nature require) by the laws of the commonwealth. For as it is uncharitable in any man to neglect the helpless, so it is in the sovereign of a commonwealth to expose them to the hazard of such uncertain charity.

But for those with strong bodies, the case is otherwise: they are to be forced to work; and to take away the excuse of not finding employment, there ought to be such laws as may encourage all kinds of arts — navigation, agriculture, fishing, and all kinds of manufacture that require labour. The multitude of the poor (and yet strong) people still increasing, they are to be transplanted into countries not sufficiently inhabited; where, nevertheless, they are not to exterminate those they find there, but to constrain them to live closer together, and not to range over a great deal of ground, snatching what they find, but to court each little plot with art and labour, to give them their sustenance in due season. And when all the world is overburdened with inhabitants, then the last remedy of all is war, which provides for every man by victory or death.

To the care of the sovereign belongs the making of good laws. But what is a good law? By a good law I do not mean a just law: for no law can be unjust. The law is made by the sovereign power, and all that is done by such power is warranted and owned by every one of the people; and what every man wills so to be, no man can say is unjust. It is in the laws of a commonwealth as in the rules of gaming: whatever the gamesters all agree on is injustice to none of them. A good law is one that is needful for the good of the people, and at the same time perspicuous.

For the use of laws (which are only rules authorised) is not to bind the people from all voluntary actions, but to direct and keep them in such a course that they do not hurt themselves by their own impetuous desires, rashness, or indiscretion — as hedges are set not to stop travellers, but to keep them in the way. So a law that is not needful, not having the true end of a law, is not good. A law may be conceived to be good when it is for the benefit of the sovereign, though it is not necessary for the people; but it is not so. For the good of the sovereign and the people cannot be separated. It is a weak sovereign that has weak subjects, and a weak people whose sovereign lacks power to rule them at his will. Unnecessary laws are not good laws, but traps for money — which, where the right of sovereign power is acknowledged, are superfluous; and where it is not acknowledged, are insufficient to defend the people.

Perspicuity consists not so much in the words of the law itself as in a declaration of the causes and motives for which it was made. That is what shows us the meaning of the legislator; and the meaning of the legislator known, the law is more easily understood by few than by many words. For all words are subject to ambiguity; and so multiplication of words in the body of the law is multiplication of ambiguity. Besides, it seems to imply (by too much diligence) that whoever can evade the words is beyond the compass of the law — and this is a cause of many unnecessary processes. For when I consider how short the laws of ancient times were, and how they grew by degrees still longer, I seem to see a contest between the framers and the pleaders of the law: the former seeking to fence the latter in, the latter seeking to evade their fences — and the pleaders have got the victory. So it belongs to the office of a legislator (such as in all commonwealths is the supreme representative, whether one man or an assembly) to make the reason perspicuous why the law was made, and to keep the body of the law itself as short, in as proper and significant terms, as may be.

It also belongs to the office of the sovereign to make a right application of punishments and rewards. And since the end of punishing is not revenge and the discharge of anger, but the correction of either the offender or, by his example, of others, the severest punishments are to be inflicted for the crimes that are of most danger to the public — such as those that proceed from malice toward the established government; those that spring from contempt of justice; those that provoke indignation in the multitude; and those that, going unpunished, seem authorised — as when they are committed by sons, servants, or favourites of men in authority. For indignation carries men not only against the doers and authors of injustice, but against any power that is likely to protect them — as in the case of Tarquin, who, for the insolent act of one of his sons, was driven out of Rome, and the monarchy itself dissolved. But for crimes of infirmity, such as those that proceed from great provocation, from great fear, great need, or from ignorance whether the act is a great crime or not, there is often room for leniency without prejudice to the commonwealth — and leniency, where there is room for it, is required by the law of nature. The punishment of the leaders and teachers in a commotion — not of the poor seduced people — when they are punished, can benefit the commonwealth by their example. To be severe to the people is to punish that ignorance which may in great part be imputed to the sovereign, whose fault it was that they were no better instructed.

In the same way, it belongs to the office and duty of the sovereign to apply his rewards always in such a way that benefit to the commonwealth may arise from them — in which consists their use and end; and this is done when those who have well served the commonwealth are, with as little expense of the common treasure as is possible, so well recompensed that others may be encouraged both to serve the same as faithfully as they can, and to study the arts by which they may be enabled to do it better. To buy with money or with preferment, from a popular ambitious subject, his being quiet and desisting from making ill impressions on the people's minds, has nothing of the nature of reward (which is ordained not for disservice but for past service), nor any sign of gratitude, but of fear; nor does it tend to the benefit but to the damage of the public. It is a contest with ambition, like that of Hercules with the monster Hydra, who, having many heads, for every one that was vanquished, three more sprang up. For in the same way, when the stubbornness of one popular man is overcome with reward, many more arise (by the example) who do the same mischief in the hope of like benefit. And as all sorts of manufacture, so also malice increases by being made vendible. And though sometimes a civil war may be deferred by such ways as that, the danger nevertheless grows greater, and the public ruin more assured. It is therefore against the duty of the sovereign, to whom the public safety is committed, to reward those who aspire to greatness by disturbing the peace of their country, and not rather to oppose the beginnings of such men with a little danger, than after a longer time with greater.

Another business of the sovereign is to choose good counsellors — I mean those whose advice he is to take in the government of the commonwealth. For this word counsel, consilium (corrupted from considium), has a wide signification, and includes all assemblies of men who sit together, not only to deliberate what is to be done in the future but also to judge of past acts, and of law for the present. I take it here in the first sense only; and in this sense there is no choice of council, neither in a democracy nor in an aristocracy, because the persons counselling are members of the person counselled. The choice of counsellors therefore belongs to monarchy; in which, the sovereign who does not endeavour to choose those who in every kind are the most able does not discharge his office as he ought. The most able counsellors are those who have least hope of benefit from giving evil counsel, and most knowledge of the things that conduce to the peace and defence of the commonwealth. It is a hard matter to know who expects benefit from public troubles; but the signs that guide to a just suspicion include the soothing of the people in their unreasonable, or irremediable, grievances by men whose estates are not sufficient to discharge their accustomed expenses — and these may easily be observed by any one whom it concerns to know it. But to know who has the most knowledge of public affairs is harder still; and those who know them need them a great deal less. For to know who knows the rules of almost any art is a great degree of the knowledge of that art, because no man can be assured of the truth of another's rules but the one who has first been taught to understand them. But the best signs of knowledge of any art are much conversing in it, and constant good effects of it. Good counsel comes not by lot, nor by inheritance; and so there is no more reason to expect good advice from the rich, or noble, in matters of state, than in delineating the dimensions of a fortress — unless we shall think there is no need of method in the study of politics (as there is in the study of geometry), but only to be onlookers; which is not so. For politics is the harder study of the two. Whereas in these parts of Europe it has been taken for a right of certain persons to have place in the highest council of state by inheritance, this is derived from the conquests of the ancient Germans, in which many absolute lords, joining together to conquer other nations, would not enter into the confederacy without such privileges as might be marks of difference in time to follow between their posterity and the posterity of their subjects — which privileges, being inconsistent with the sovereign power, they may seem to keep by the favour of the sovereign; but contending for them as their right, they must inevitably, by degrees, let them go, and have at last no further honour than naturally adheres to their abilities.

And however able the counsellors in any matter may be, the benefit of their counsel is greater when they give each their advice, and the reasons of it, apart, than when they do it in an assembly by way of orations; and when they have premeditated, than when they speak on the sudden. Both because they have more time to survey the consequences of action, and because they are less subject to being carried away into contradiction through envy, emulation, or other passions arising from the difference of opinion.

The best counsel, in those things that concern not other nations but only the ease and benefit the subjects may enjoy by laws that look only inward, is to be taken from the general information and complaints of the people of each province, who are best acquainted with their own wants; and so, when they demand nothing in derogation of the essential rights of sovereignty, they ought to be diligently taken notice of. For without those essential rights (as I have often said before) the commonwealth cannot at all subsist.

A commander-in-chief of an army, if he is not popular, shall neither be loved nor feared as he ought to be by his army, and consequently cannot perform that office with good success. He must therefore be industrious, valiant, affable, generous, and fortunate, that he may gain an opinion both of sufficiency and of loving his soldiers. This is popularity; and it breeds in the soldiers both the desire and the courage to recommend themselves to his favour, and protects the severity of the general in punishing (when need is) mutinous or negligent soldiers. But this love of soldiers (if security is not given of the commander's fidelity) is a dangerous thing to sovereign power, especially when it is in the hands of an unpopular assembly. So it belongs to the safety of the people both that they be good leaders, and faithful subjects, to whom the sovereign commits his armies.

But when the sovereign himself is popular — that is, revered and loved by his people — there is no danger at all from the popularity of a subject. For soldiers are never so generally unjust as to side with their captain (even when they love him) against their sovereign, when they love not only his person but also his cause. So those who have at any time, by violence, suppressed the power of their lawful sovereign, before they could settle themselves in his place, have always had the trouble of contriving titles, to save the people from the shame of receiving them. To have a known right to sovereign power is so popular a quality that the one who has it, for his own part, needs no more, to turn the hearts of his subjects to him, than that they see him able absolutely to govern his own family — nor, on the part of his enemies, more than a disbanding of their armies. For the greatest and most active part of mankind has never until now been well contented with the present.

Concerning the offices of one sovereign toward another (which are comprehended in that law commonly called the law of nations), I need not say anything in this place; because the law of nations and the law of nature are the same thing. And every sovereign has the same right, in procuring the safety of his people, that any private man can have in procuring the safety of his own body. The same law that dictates to men who have no civil government what they ought to do, and what to avoid, with respect to one another, dictates the same to commonwealths — that is, to the consciences of sovereign princes and sovereign assemblies; there being no court of natural justice but in the conscience only, where not man, but God, reigns. His laws (such of them as oblige all mankind), in respect of God as the author of nature, are natural; and in respect of the same God as king of kings, are laws. But of the kingdom of God, both as king of kings and as king also of a peculiar people, I shall speak in the rest of this discourse.
